home-remodeling.h1: The Grove's houses deserve better bones
home-remodeling.hero_sub: PGX Builders Group takes Coconut Grove homes down to the good bones and rebuilds them properly — full permits through the City of Miami, daily supervision, and one licensed contractor (CGC1539072) accountable for all of it.
intro_paragraphs: Coconut Grove is Miami's oldest neighborhood, and its houses show every era of it: Bahamian-rooted cottages near Charles Avenue, 1920s Mediterranean homes in Center Grove, mid-century ranches in Natoma Manors, and gated bayfront estates off Main Highway in South Grove. Owners here rarely want a teardown. They want the house they bought, opened up and rebuilt to current standards — new layouts, structural openings, full electrical and plumbing replacement, impact windows, and finishes that stand up to Grove humidity without losing the character that made the street worth living on.

Permits run through the City of Miami Building Department, and the Grove adds its own layer: most residential streets sit inside the NCD-2 or NCD-3 conservation overlays, which regulate setbacks, massing, and — famously — trees. Demolition work in NCD-3 carries its own review and tree-survey requirements, and removing canopy triggers the city's tree ordinance and its replacement math. Add Miami-Dade's High-Velocity Hurricane Zone product approvals for every new window and door, and a Grove remodel involves real paperwork. We handle it because we have been filing it for years.

PGX Builders Group works at the top of this market, and it shows in how we run a job. You get a fixed written scope before demolition starts, a supervisor on site every day, and protection for the floors, plaster, and landscaping that are staying. In gated communities like The Moorings or Hughes Cove we keep crews tight, parking legal, and neighbors unbothered. One team carries the project from estimate through final inspection and warranty — 100% permitted, 100% inspected, no orphaned punch list.

faqs.q: Do I need special approvals to remodel a home in Coconut Grove?
faqs.a: For interior work, a standard City of Miami permit with trade permits and inspections usually covers it. Exterior changes, demolition, and anything touching trees bring the Grove's conservation overlays into play: NCD-3 demolition work gets added scrutiny, including an arborist's tree survey, and tree removals need their own permits with replacement planting. We tell you which reviews your project triggers before you commit to it, not after.

faqs.q: How long does a whole-home remodel take in Coconut Grove?
faqs.a: Longer than a spec-house flip, honestly. Design and engineering take a few months, City of Miami permitting takes its share, and construction on a full-gut remodel of a substantial Grove home typically runs the better part of a year, sometimes more. We commit to a written schedule with the scope, then run daily supervision to defend it. Owners who plan realistic timelines end up far happier than owners who plan optimistic ones.

faqs.q: Can you modernize an older Grove house without erasing its character?
faqs.a: That is most of our work here. The shell, the proportions, the original details worth saving — those stay and get restored. Everything behind them gets replaced: wiring, plumbing, ductwork, insulation, and windows upgraded to impact-rated units that suit the facade. A 1920s house with 2020s systems is the whole point of remodeling in Coconut Grove rather than tearing down and starting over.

faqs.q: What does a whole-home remodel cost in Coconut Grove?
faqs.a: It depends on scope more than square footage — structural changes, the level of finish, and how much of the systems get replaced. We work at the high end of the market, and we would rather show you a detailed fixed scope than quote a teaser number that grows later. What we can promise is that the price you sign is the price we defend, with any changes documented in writing.

faqs.q: Will the protected trees on my lot complicate the project?
faqs.a: They will shape it, which is different. Coconut Grove's canopy is protected by the City of Miami's tree ordinance, and the NCD rules exist partly to keep it standing. We design staging, access, and any exterior work around root-protection zones, and when a removal is genuinely unavoidable we handle the permit and the required replacement planting. Most remodels never need to touch a tree at all.

kitchen-remodeling.h1: Grove kitchens, opened up at last
kitchen-remodeling.hero_sub: Custom cabinetry, stone counters, and real layout changes for Coconut Grove kitchens — designed, permitted through the City of Miami, and built under daily supervision by a licensed general contractor.
intro_paragraphs: Most Coconut Grove kitchens were designed for a different century. The 1920s houses in Center Grove and the North Grove blocks off Tigertail Avenue were built with kitchens meant to be closed off; the mid-century homes in Natoma Manors got galley layouts that ignore how anyone cooks now. What Grove owners actually order is a structural fix: walls opened to the living space, an island with seating, custom cabinetry run to the ceiling, and stone chosen slab by slab. The kitchen becomes the room the house is organized around, which is what it should have been all along.

Kitchen remodels in Coconut Grove are permitted through the City of Miami Building Department — building, electrical, plumbing, and mechanical, each with its own inspections. The good news: an interior kitchen stays clear of most of the Grove's NCD conservation review, which concerns itself with exteriors and trees. The catch is structural. Opening a bearing wall between kitchen and living room needs an engineer's calculations and a permit that reflects them, and moving a gas range across the room brings its own trade permits. We file complete drawings the first time, which is the quiet secret to decent timelines.

PGX builds kitchens the way the rest of a high-end Grove house deserves: a fixed written scope, cabinetry ordered to the millimeter, and a site supervisor there every day the crew is. We template stone after cabinets are set, not before, and we protect the oak floors and everything else staying put. From first measurement to final inspection you deal with one accountable team — licensed, insured, CGC1539072 — not a parade of subcontractors managing themselves.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remodel a kitchen in Coconut Grove?
faqs.a: Yes. Kitchen remodels in the Grove are permitted through the City of Miami, and anything involving electrical, plumbing, gas, or structural changes requires trade permits and inspections. Skipping them is tempting for a simple update; it is also how homes fail scrutiny at resale, and unpermitted work in a market this examined is expensive to unwind. We pull every permit and close every inspection, because that is the product.

faqs.q: Can you remove the wall between my kitchen and living room?
faqs.a: In most Grove houses, yes. Many of those walls are load-bearing, which means an engineer sizes a beam, the city reviews the calculations, and the load path gets built and inspected properly. It is routine work when done in the right order and a sagging ceiling when it is not. We have opened floor plans in houses from every era the Grove has, and the sequence always starts with engineering.

faqs.q: How long does a custom kitchen remodel take?
faqs.a: The honest driver is cabinetry. Custom cabinet packages carry real lead times, so we sequence design, selections, and permitting while they are in production. Once demolition starts, a full kitchen with layout changes generally runs a few months of construction. The expensive mistake is demolishing before the cabinets are ordered — you pay for that gap by living without a kitchen. We do not run jobs that way.

faqs.q: What does a high-end kitchen cost in Coconut Grove?
faqs.a: Custom cabinetry and natural stone drive the number more than anything else, followed by appliances and how far the layout moves. We are not the cheap bid and do not pretend to be; we compete on the finished product and on a fixed written scope that keeps the number honest. Bring us your wish list and we will price it line by line so you can decide with real information.

faqs.q: Will my kitchen project trigger Coconut Grove's NCD or tree rules?
faqs.a: A purely interior kitchen usually stays clear of NCD design review, which concentrates on exteriors, demolition, and canopy. The exceptions matter, though: enlarging a window, adding a door to the garden, or running new exterior venting can bring the overlay and HVHZ product approvals into scope. We flag those triggers during design, so nothing surprises you at the permit counter.

bathroom-remodeling.h1: Stone, steam, and waterproofing done right
bathroom-remodeling.hero_sub: PGX Builders Group builds primary suites and guest baths across Coconut Grove — fully permitted, supervised daily, and waterproofed like South Florida humidity is a given, because it is.
bathroom-remodeling.local_heading: What Grove bathrooms are up against
intro_paragraphs: A bathroom in an older Coconut Grove house is usually the room that gives the house's age away first. Behind the tile in a 1920s Center Grove Mediterranean or a Bay Heights ranch you will typically find original cast-iron drains, undersized supply lines, and framing that has spent decades in humidity. High-end owners here treat bathroom remodels as small construction projects, not decorating exercises: gut to the studs, replace the plumbing back to the stack, then build the marble shower and freestanding tub on top of work that will not leak into the room below.

Bathroom permits in Coconut Grove go through the City of Miami Building Department, with plumbing and electrical rough inspections before anything closes up — which is exactly the order you want, since covered-up shortcuts are how bathrooms fail. Interior bath work generally avoids the Grove's NCD design review, but swap a window in the shower wall and you are into Miami-Dade HVHZ territory: impact-rated, code-approved, ideally obscured glass. In bayfront homes we also watch the FEMA substantial-improvement math when a bath remodel is part of a larger renovation.

Our bathrooms are built in the unglamorous order that makes them last: slope, pan, membrane, flood test, then stone. PGX supervises daily, holds a fixed written scope, and treats the rest of your house as off-limits — floors protected, dust contained, one bathroom's demolition never becoming the whole home's problem. You get one licensed, insured team (CGC1539072) from estimate to warranty, and tile layouts you approved on paper before anyone opened a box.

faqs.q: Do bathroom remodels in Coconut Grove require permits?
faqs.a: Yes — through the City of Miami, with plumbing and electrical rough inspections before walls close. That sequence is your protection: the inspector and our supervisor both see the work while it can still be corrected easily. In older Grove houses, the permit process also surfaces the aging cast iron and undersized wiring that a cosmetic remodel would have tiled over and left for the next owner to discover.

faqs.q: Should I replace the original plumbing while remodeling a 1920s house?
faqs.a: Almost always. Cast-iron drains from that era are at or past the end of their service life, and the walls will never be cheaper to open than during your remodel. Replacing supply and drain lines back to the stack adds modest cost now and removes the most common cause of the leak that ruins a finished bathroom later. We consider it the least optional line in the scope.

faqs.q: How long does a full bathroom remodel take?
faqs.a: For a gut renovation of a primary bath, plan on several weeks of construction once permits and materials are in hand, longer when walls move or plumbing relocates. Stone, glass, and fixtures carry lead times, so we order before demolition, not after. The flood test in the middle is non-negotiable and occasionally adds a day. It is the cheapest day in the whole project.

faqs.q: What does a high-end bathroom remodel cost in Coconut Grove?
faqs.a: The range is wide because the choices are: book-matched stone and unlacquered brass live at a different number than porcelain and chrome. Waterproofing, plumbing replacement, and proper glass are the constants we will not thin out to hit a price. We give you a fixed written scope with the real number attached — and at this level, the bathroom you get should embarrass the one it replaced.

faqs.q: Can you add or enlarge a window in my bathroom?
faqs.a: Usually, and in a shaded Grove bathroom it is often the best money in the project. An exterior opening means impact-rated glass approved for Miami-Dade's High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, a permit reflecting the structural change, and — depending on your street — attention to the NCD overlay. Obscured impact glass solves privacy without curtains. We handle the engineering and approvals as part of the scope.

home-additions.hero_sub: Rear extensions, second stories, and garage conversions across Coconut Grove — engineered, permitted through the City of Miami, and supervised daily by PGX Builders Group, licensed general contractor CGC1539072.
home-additions.local_heading: Adding on without giving up the Grove
intro_paragraphs: Coconut Grove lots come with two things owners refuse to lose: mature trees and the feel of the street. So instead of tearing down, owners in Center Grove, Natoma Manors, and the avenues off Tigertail add on — a rear extension toward the garden, a second story over the original footprint, a garage turned guest suite. Done well, an addition buys the square footage a growing household needs while the oaks, the setbacks, and the house the neighbors have known for decades stay put. Done badly, it reads as a box stapled to a bungalow. The difference is design and structure.

Additions are where the Grove's rulebook earns its reputation. Permits go through the City of Miami, and the NCD-3 conservation overlay governs setbacks, massing, and how much of the lot you may cover — while the city's tree ordinance protects the canopy your new footprint has to negotiate with. Any demolition tied to the project brings its own review before permits issue. Near the bayfront, FEMA flood maps and the substantial-improvement rule can shape what is worth building. None of this is a reason not to add on. It is a reason to hire someone fluent in it.

PGX approaches an addition as structural work first: foundations that respect root-protection zones, tie-beams and connections engineered for the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, and a roofline that joins the original house instead of colliding with it. You get a fixed written scope, a supervisor on site every day, and an occupied-home plan that keeps the existing house livable, clean, and secure while the new one grows behind it. One team, estimate through warranty — the way 150+ South Florida remodels and additions have taught us to run it.

faqs.q: What do the NCD-3 rules mean for my addition?
faqs.a: NCD-3 is the conservation overlay covering most of residential Coconut Grove, and it governs the things an addition lives or dies on: setbacks, massing, how much lot you can cover, and the trees your new footprint must respect. Demolition connected to the work is reviewed on its own track, tree survey included. We run a feasibility check against the overlay before design money gets spent, so you know what the lot allows first.

faqs.q: Can I add a second story to my Coconut Grove home?
faqs.a: Often, yes — and on tree-covered Grove lots, up is frequently the only direction with room. It starts with a structural evaluation: the existing foundation and walls must carry the new load, or be upgraded until they can, with everything engineered for the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone. The overlay's height and massing rules apply, and making the new floor look inevitable rather than added is a design problem we take seriously.

faqs.q: Will the trees on my lot limit where I can build?
faqs.a: They are the first thing we survey. Coconut Grove's canopy is protected by the City of Miami's tree ordinance, so the addition's footprint, foundations, and construction access all get planned around root-protection zones. When a conflict is real, removal requires a permit and replacement planting, and approval is never guaranteed. In practice, designing with the trees usually produces a better addition than the one the original sketch imagined.

faqs.q: How long does an addition take from first call to finished room?
faqs.a: Count the phases honestly: a few months for design and engineering, the permitting process through the City of Miami and any overlay review, then construction — typically several months to a year depending on whether you are extending back or going up. We give you a written schedule tied to the fixed scope and supervise daily to hold it. Anyone quoting dramatically faster is skipping a phase you will miss later.

faqs.q: Does the FEMA substantial-improvement rule affect additions near the bay?
faqs.a: It can. In mapped flood zones along the Grove's bayfront, federal rules compare the value of improvements against the value of the existing structure; cross the threshold and the whole building may need to be brought into compliance with current flood elevation requirements. That math can genuinely change what is worth building. We assess it early for any waterfront project, so the budget reflects reality from day one.

outdoor-living.title: Outdoor Living & Exteriors in Coconut Grove FL | PGX Builders
outdoor-living.meta_description: Terraces, summer kitchens, pergolas, and exterior upgrades built under the Coconut Grove canopy by a licensed Miami GC. Call PGX at (786) 273-2524.
outdoor-living.hero_sub: PGX designs and builds terraces, summer kitchens, and full exterior upgrades for Coconut Grove homes — permitted through the City of Miami, engineered for hurricanes, and supervised by us daily.
intro_paragraphs: Nobody in Coconut Grove wants a backyard that fights the trees — the canopy is why people move here. In South Grove and gated enclaves like Entrada Estates and Camp Biscayne, outdoor projects are built into the shade, not instead of it: stone terraces set between oaks, summer kitchens under proper roofs, pergolas that filter what sun the canopy allows through, and pools worked into lots that are rarely flat or simple. The best Grove exteriors feel like the garden was always going to end up this way. That takes planning, not luck.

Exterior work is where Coconut Grove's rules concentrate. Permits run through the City of Miami, the NCD conservation overlays care about what you build and what you pave, and the city's tree ordinance means root-zone work or any removal near a protected tree needs a permit and, usually, replacement planting. Structures like pergolas and summer-kitchen roofs must be engineered for Miami-Dade's High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, and in the bayfront blocks, drainage and flood elevation deserve attention before pavers do. We design around all of it and file the paperwork first.

Outdoor projects fail on coordination more than craft — the trades stack up: concrete, gas, electrical, roofing, stone, landscape. PGX runs them under one fixed written scope with a supervisor on site daily, protecting the lawn, the irrigation, and the driveway you are keeping. In guard-gated communities we register crews properly and work clean, because in the Grove your contractor's conduct is part of your reputation. Licensed and insured, CGC1539072, one accountable team from estimate to warranty.

faqs.q: Do I need permits for a pergola or summer kitchen in Coconut Grove?
faqs.a: Yes. Structures are permitted through the City of Miami and engineered for High-Velocity Hurricane Zone wind loads — a pergola that is not anchored for hurricanes is a projectile with a paperwork problem. Summer kitchens add gas, electrical, and sometimes plumbing permits. Depending on your street, the NCD overlay may weigh in on exterior changes. We file all of it before breaking ground.

faqs.q: Can you build around the big oaks without hurting them?
faqs.a: That is the defining skill of Grove exterior work. Protected trees mean root zones we do not trench through, grade changes we avoid, and hardscape designed to breathe near trunks. Any pruning or removal near a protected tree goes through the city's tree permitting, usually with replacement planting attached. A terrace that kills the oak shading it is a failure regardless of how good the stonework is.

faqs.q: What outdoor materials hold up under the Grove's canopy?
faqs.a: Shade plus South Florida humidity is hard on outdoor finishes: mildew, leaf stain, and slow drying punish porous stone and cheap sealers. We favor dense stone or porcelain pavers, marine-grade stainless in summer kitchens, and woods or composites rated for moisture. Just as important is drainage — a terrace that sheds water quickly stays clean, and one that puddles under leaf litter never looks finished.

faqs.q: How disruptive is a full exterior renovation?
faqs.a: Less than you would expect when it is sequenced properly. We phase the work so you keep access to the house, contain the mess to defined zones, protect irrigation and landscape that stays, and hold to reasonable work hours. In guard-gated communities like The Moorings or Entrada Estates we coordinate crews and vehicles with security in advance. The supervisor on site daily is what keeps all of that true.

faqs.q: Can PGX coordinate re-roofing and impact windows with exterior work?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is usually smarter to bundle them. Re-roofing, impact windows and doors, stucco, and paint share scaffolding, sequencing, and inspections, so combining them costs less disruption than doing each alone a year apart. Every product carries Miami-Dade approvals for the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, and one team owns the schedule and the warranty rather than three vendors pointing at each other.

permitting-compliance.local_heading: What the Grove's permits actually involve
intro_paragraphs: Coconut Grove has been building on the same streets for well over a century, which means nearly every house here carries a permit history — and some of that history was never finished. A 1920s Mediterranean in Center Grove, a bungalow off Charles Avenue in Village West, a mid-century ranch in Natoma Manors, a bayfront house in The Moorings: any of them can be dragging an open or expired permit from a prior owner, pulled for a roof, a pool enclosure, a window swap or an addition, and then abandoned. It surfaces in a title search weeks before a closing or a refinance, and it stops the deal cold.

Coconut Grove sits inside the City of Miami, so permits are filed with the City of Miami Building Department through its iBuild permitting system, under Miami 21 zoning and the Coconut Grove neighborhood conservation district overlays that shape setbacks, tree canopy and street frontage. Designated historic properties add a certificate of appropriateness from the Historic and Environmental Preservation Board. Every exterior window, door and roof system needs a Miami-Dade product approval for the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, submitted with the drawings. Houses on the low ground near the bay pick up flood-zone review, and the condominium buildings along South Bayshore Drive carry recertification and milestone obligations of their own.

PGX Builders Group is a licensed general contractor, not a permit runner, and the distinction matters when a permit has to be closed rather than merely opened. We read the property's permit record first, tell you plainly what is outstanding and what finishing it will take, and coordinate the architect, engineer or arborist the file genuinely needs. Scope goes in writing before anything starts. A supervisor meets every inspector on site rather than leaving a lockbox and hoping. One team carries it from first application to final approval — 100% permitted, 100% inspected, and documented so the next title search comes back clean.

faqs.q: A title search on my Coconut Grove house found an open permit. What now?
faqs.a: An open or expired permit does not disappear with the sale. It follows the property, and the title company will hold your closing until it is resolved. We pull the record, work out whether the work was actually done, and take the file over with a completion permit and a change of contractor if the original one is long gone. Concealed work sometimes needs an engineer's letter. Then we call inspections and get the final signed. Weeks, not days — start well before your closing date.

faqs.q: Which office issues building permits for Coconut Grove?
faqs.a: The City of Miami Building Department. Coconut Grove is a City of Miami neighborhood rather than its own village, so applications and plans run through the city's iBuild system. Zoning is Miami 21, with the Coconut Grove neighborhood conservation district overlays layered on top, and the Historic and Environmental Preservation Board involved where a property is designated. Behind all of it sits Miami-Dade County, whose product approvals govern anything installed in the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone.

faqs.q: Does a small job in the Grove really need a permit?
faqs.a: More of them do than owners expect. Structural, electrical, plumbing and mechanical work, roofing, windows and doors, pools, decks, fences, driveways and most exterior changes all require one, and tree work needs its own. Painting and swapping cabinet doors generally do not. The jobs that cause trouble later are precisely the ones people skip: a window replacement, a rebuilt bathroom, a summer kitchen, a garage quietly turned into a bedroom. Unpermitted work shows up as a gap between the county property card and the house.

faqs.q: Our building on South Bayshore Drive got a recertification notice. Can you handle the repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. The inspection itself belongs to a licensed engineer or architect, and we coordinate that rather than pretend to do it. Our part is the work the report calls for: concrete and stucco restoration, waterproofing, balcony and railing repairs, electrical corrections, and the permits and inspections that close it all out. Miami-Dade recertification, the state milestone inspection for buildings three habitable stories and taller, and the structural integrity reserve study tend to surface the same list. We price it as a written scope, not a guess.

faqs.q: What does it cost to get an old permit closed out?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on what sits behind the permit. If the work was done properly and only the final inspection was missed, reopening and finishing the file is a modest exercise. If the work was never completed, was done badly, or is buried behind finishes that now have to be opened up, the cost is the repair, not the paperwork. We review the record and the house before quoting, and we tell you which of those two situations you are in before you spend anything.
